Geopolitics & Diplomacy.title: Both blocs claim upper hand in crucial Israeli election | First Thing
Geopolitics & Diplomacy.text: Benjamin Netanyahu vows to form new coalition while opposition bloc leader says result shows prime minister should step down. Plus, a scathing review of Elon Musk’s AI-generated version of The OdysseyGood morning. Israel could be in for weeks of political haggling after exit polls and partial official results showed neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition bloc led by the former general Gadi Eisenkot had won enough seats to form a government.With 70% of the vote, or 4m ballots, counted so far, the Netanyahu bloc had 54 seats, the Eisenkot-led Change bloc 47 seats, and the Palestinian parties 19 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed for a majority.What have the two leaders said so far? Israel’s longest-serving prime minister vowed to assemble a coalition through agreements between his Likud party, far-right factions and Jewish religious parties. Eisenkot had said earlier in the evening that “people decided in favour of change” and Netanyahu should have “announced today his retirement from politics”.What does the increase in the Palestinian bloc mean? The election was marked by a record participation by Israeli citizens of Palestinian origin, a discriminated minority that makes up about 20% of the country’s population. Julian Borger explains from Nazareth that Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing. Millions of other Palestinians living under Israeli rule in the occupied West Bank and Gaza cannot vote.Here is what we know about the declared results so far. Our live coverage continues on the website.What else has Trump been saying about fossil fuels? Artificial Intelligence.title: Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
Artificial Intelligence.text: This article is brought to you by VicOne.A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal.But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path.In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation.At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe.How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behaviorA robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models, a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task.In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement.VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did.  In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack.VicOneSafety-related decisions have inputs tooAn independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated?At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved.A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall.Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information.  Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm.VicOneDeliberate attacks challenge safety assumptionsA safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed.Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research, a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once.Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated.Security testing strengthens robot safety evidenceSafety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated.That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots. IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems. The EU Machinery Regulation, which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions.  Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOneBefore deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team.VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community, VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. VicOne’s Radeis helps teams validate potential effects before deployment, while Rthena provides visibility into risks and behavior during operation.Five questions safety and security teams should answer togetherThe central test is whether a robot’s safeguards still protect people when the information they rely on is manipulated. Safety and security teams can begin by tracing the inputs behind each protective decision, challenging them, and revisiting the evidence as the robot changes. They can start with these five questions:1. What does each protective function read? Map the readings, estimates, messages, and confirmations. Identify which safeguards operate independently of the robot’s AI decisions.2. How does that information arrive? Check how inputs are produced, transmitted, authenticated where appropriate, and handled when they are missing or implausible.3. What happens if an input is manipulated? Test false distances, drifting position estimates, and other relevant scenarios against the robot’s safety limits.4. Can one action mislead several inputs? Check whether sensor fusion or seemingly independent safeguards share a point of failure.5. When should the evidence be revisited? Reassess after changes to software, models, sensors, or operating conditions. Agree on bounded responses to suspicious behavior with the safety team in advance.The goal is not only to show that a protective function works. Teams also need evidence that it remains protective when the information behind its decision is wrong or deliberately manipulated — and that another safeguard can catch the resulting hazard when needed. As robots change, that evidence needs to change with them.For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

Artificial Intelligence.title: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
Artificial Intelligence.text: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to PublishTwo Ways to Make a Paper With AII took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed.What Gave Away My AI Papers Round 1: The Fake PaperCreated with free versions of ChatGPT and GeminiGhost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.Round 2: The AI-Research PaperCreated by the autonomous research system FARSToo many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”Blurred LinesMy homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.Round 2: Using an AI Science EngineFARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.Round 2: Attempt to PublishBecause FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.Automation Changing the LandscapeAutomated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future?Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.See the AI-Generated PapersBenjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Art & Culture.title: Maison Margiela and NUDAKE Serve Tea With a Deconstructed Twist
Art & Culture.text: SummaryMaison Margiela and NUDAKE reinterpret tea rituals through deconstructed porcelain and shared forms.Bianchetto finishes, warped rims and joined saucers define the “OOPS” aesthetic.The collection launches October 30 at NUDAKE TEAHOUSE in Seoul.Maison Margiela and NUDAKE are turning tea time into an exercise in controlled imperfection. Dubbed “OOPS,” the pair’s first collaboration takes the Maison’s deconstructive codes away from fashion and applies them to porcelain, tea and the ritual of sharing a pot.Much of the collection is washed in Margiela’s signature Bianchetto treatment, giving otherwise familiar tea objects a deliberately unfinished, timeworn character. A sculptural teapot anchors the range with a metal ring at its lid and the house’s recognizable four-stitch detail pressed into its body, while accompanying cups distort the expected symmetry of traditional teaware through gently warped rims and a joined double saucer intended for two.That idea of two people sharing one experience runs through more than the ceramics. NUDAKE’s accompanying Oops black tea takes inspiration from the image of a dark crimson plum being crushed beneath a leather shoe, translating the scene into a blend layered with delicate herbs, sweet fruit and earthy notes. An Oops Tea Bag physically joins two sachets together so that two cups can be steeped at once, while two limited Oops Loose Leaf editions extend the blend into collectible tins.A co-branded tea tumbler rounds out the functional pieces, carrying the same pared-back white finish into a more everyday format. Across the collection, Margiela’s preference for disrupting archetypes meets NUDAKE’s more playful approach to food and sensory design, making the smallest irregularities — a crooked rim, an exposed stitch or a shared saucer — central to the experience.Maison Margiela x NUDAKE “OOPS” launches on October 30, 2026 at 11 a.m. KST, with the collection offered through the NUDAKE TEAHOUSE at HAUS NOWHERE SEOUL in Seongsu-dong. The release will also be accompanied by an installation built from roughly 1,500 glasses and a glass-harp performance by Polish artists GlassDuo, extending the collaboration’s themes of chance, sound and imperfect beauty into the surrounding space. Art & Culture.title: Japanese Artisans Rework Vintage Polo Ralph Lauren for Reimagined Collection at PoloFest Tokyo
Art & Culture.text: SummaryPolo Ralph Lauren has showcased its Reimagined collection at the inaugural PoloFest celebration in TokyoJapanese craftspeople including Yui Narita and Mitsugu Sasaki utilized traditional boro mending and embroidery across archival Polo silhouettesEach reworked piece is offered through a charity raffle with all proceeds benefiting Ralph Lauren's Pink Pony cancer initiativePolo Ralph Lauren has officially presented its one-of-a-kind "Reimagined" collection during the inaugural PoloFest activation in Tokyo. The installation brings together prominent Japanese artisans to breathe new life into vintage Polo garments using traditional mending and restoration techniques.The collection repurposes pre-worn garments into tactile, textured works of art. Key pieces on display include classic chinos embroidered with smiley face emoji patterns, heavily patchworked ties and hats rebuilt with layered fabric scraps, and distressed denim baseball caps stitched with individual red felt letters spelling out "RALPH." The initiative highlights master craftspeople such as Yui Narita, founder of Osaka vintage store Brown Tabby Works, alongside Mitsugu Sasaki of Sasaki Yōhinten, who applied the traditional Japanese practice of boro to repair and reinforce garments through hand-sewn fabric layering.The showcase directly reflects Ralph Lauren’s personal reverence for well-loved clothing, echoing the designer's philosophy that "where wear becomes character, repair becomes art, and every stitch creates a new patina." Serving as the opening activation ahead of the brand's 60th anniversary in 2027, the three-day PoloFest gathering honors Japan’s longstanding connection to the label since its arrival in 1976, celebrating decades of local craftsmanship and classic Americana.The Polo Ralph Lauren Reimagined pieces are available exclusively via charity raffle at PoloFest Tokyo, with all proceeds directly supporting the Pink Pony initiative to fight cancer.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

This season, that dialogue takes inspiration from the spirit of 1980s London, a period of cultural convergence and youthful experimentation that also informs the accompanying campaign, photographed by Harley Weir.At the heart of the ready-to-wear offering is a premium leather blouson in Wales Bonner's signature bark color, distinguished by crochet side stripes and subtle tonal embossed branding. Its refined construction sets the tone for a collection that moves between tailored elegance and the relaxed familiarity of athletic uniforms. A double-knit jersey tracksuit offers a more traditional interpretation of sportswear, while a pinstripe track top and matching shorts introduce a sartorial twist to the classic coordinated set.Elsewhere, a collared football top with matching trousers draws on vintage sporting references, translating the familiar codes of football apparel into a more considered everyday silhouette. The interplay between structured and relaxed dressing gives the collection a distinct sense of versatility, allowing individual pieces to move beyond their original sporting associations.Completing the apparel lineup are stirrup-detailed track pants, a long-sleeve knit and double-logo T-shirts, alongside accessories such as a neoprene bag with crocodile leather-inspired paneling, a lanyard and two pairs of socks. The accompanying footwear lineup includes the crocodile-stamped WB Karintha and WB Gazelle Snake, the suede-crafted WB ADIZERO Adios Suede, and the newly introduced WB BW Pony. These silhouettes extend the collection's focus on tactile materials and archival reinterpretation through crocodile-embossed leather, suede, pony hair and lizard-print detailing.The adidas Originals by Wales Bonner FW26 collection is scheduled to launch globally on October 29 via adidas.com, the CONFIRMED app and select retailers.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: adidas Originals Unveils the ADAPTIK ONE Carabiner Watch
Entertainment.text: Summaryadidas Originals launched the ADAPTIK ONE, a convertible 2-way carabiner wristwatch.The 38mm aluminum timepiece features a digital display and silicone band.Priced at ¥20,900 JPY (APPROX. $132 USD), the versatile watch drops on November 27.adidas Originals is rethinking where a watch needs to be worn with the new ADAPTIK ONE, a digital timepiece that shifts between a conventional wristwatch and a carabiner-style hanging watch.Built around a clean 38mm square aluminum case, the design pairs a digital display with a color-matched silicone strap for a lightweight, sport-inflected look that leans naturally into the label’s streetwear vocabulary. A sliding mechanism allows the watch head to be transferred to the included carabiner attachment, letting it hang from a belt loop, bag or other accessories rather than remaining fixed to the wrist. The lineup spans three references in blue, black and green, giving the functional concept a simple color-led identity.Underneath the playful format, the ADAPTIK ONE keeps its specifications deliberately straightforward, using a battery-powered digital quartz movement alongside stopwatch, calendar and backlight functions, with a 38mm-wide, 11.5mm-thick case weighing approximately 45 grams and offering 3 ATM water resistance.More than a conventional watch with an interchangeable strap, the design treats the timepiece as a wearable accessory that can move between the wrist and clothing depending on the styling. Each of the three colorways is officially priced at ¥20,900 JPY (approx. $132 USD), the adidas Originals ADAPTIK ONE is scheduled to release in Japan on November 27, 2026 via the brand's website.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Instagram Challenges YouTube With New 90-Minute Longform Video Uploads
Entertainment.text: SummaryInstagram has begun testing a new upload format dubbed Features allowing creators to share longform videos up to 90 minutes in lengthThe initiative aims to connect short-form Reels with in-depth video content optimized for mobile viewing and the Instagram TV appCurrently undergoing trials in Brazil the test is slated to expand to select creators across the United StatesInstagram has officially begun testing "Features", a new upload format enabling creators to share longform videos up to 90 minutes in length. The move marks a strategic shift toward extended media after years of prioritizing short-form video.The feature represents Instagram’s most notable longform endeavor since sunsetting IGTV. Explaining the pivot, Instagram VP of Product Tessa Lyons noted, "Reels is still going to be a core part of Instagram. But when you want to go deeper with the creators you love and the content that they’re creating, you should be able to do that on Instagram.” To build an interconnected system, the platform is testing "Clips as Reels," allowing creators to turn snippets into links pointing to full-length uploads, alongside options to push playback directly to the Instagram TV app.Addressing the strategy, Instagram head Adam Mosseri shared, “The thing that the team has been working on that we’re excited to share with you is trying to make it so that the short-form and the long-form video can be symbiotic. We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app... I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long term.”Currently undergoing trials in Brazil, testing for "Features" and "Clips as Reels" will soon expand to select creators across the United States. Entertainment.title: ‘Resident Evil’ Could End Within the Next Decade
Entertainment.text: SummaryResident Evil producer Jun Takeuchi reveals the overarching story may conclude within ten years.Resident Evil: Requiem recently capped off Capcom’s initial ten-year strategic roadmap.Multiple future titles will definitively wrap up the iconic survival horror franchise arcs.Resident Evil may finally have an endgame in sight — at least for the overarching story Capcom has been building across its modern games. Speaking in an interview originally published by Yahoo Japan, franchise executive producer Jun Takeuchi revealed that the current narrative could reach its conclusion within the next decade.Takeuchi explained that Capcom began developing a 10-year strategy while planning 2019’s Resident Evil 2 remake, with the order of subsequent remakes and mainline entries forming part of a broader direction for the series. With Resident Evil Requiem arriving earlier this year, Takeuchi said he considers that first decade-long phase effectively complete, adding that he expects the larger storyline to reach its conclusion during the next 10 years. His comments refer specifically to the ongoing narrative rather than suggesting Capcom intends to retire the Resident Evil franchise altogether.That conclusion is unlikely to arrive through a single final game. Takeuchi confirmed that Capcom has “multiple titles” planned before reaching that point, although he stopped short of revealing how many or what shape the remaining story will take. The comments add further context to the company’s modern approach to Resident Evil, which has developed along parallel tracks through new numbered installments and remakes of earlier entries, with Takeuchi noting that the series’ wider narrative was never completely mapped out from the beginning but instead expanded with each release.Following the resurgence that began with 2017’s Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, Capcom has alternated between new chapters and reinterpretations of its back catalog, most recently culminating in Requiem. The next confirmed project is Resident Evil: Code Veronica, a remake of Code: Veronica currently scheduled for 2027, suggesting there remains plenty of ground to cover before the franchise’s present storyline reaches its eventual endpoint.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: First Look at Nike’s Ovolo 2.0 Sneaker-Heel Hybrid Revival
Entertainment.text: Name: Nike Ovolo 2.0SKU: TBCRelease Date: Holiday 2026Nike is continuing its streak of reviving obscure, experimental designs from the mid-2000s with a first look at the highly unusual Nike Ovolo 2.0. Revealed by Nike via its latest SNKRS Verified product preview, the upcoming model re-engineers a seldom-seen sneaker heel originally introduced in 2004.Slated to arrive exclusively in women's sizing for the Holiday 2026 season, the Ovolo 2.0 will debut in two bold colorways: a sleek, monochromatic "Black" and a futuristic "Metallic Silver." The Ovolo 2.0 functions as a striking hybrid, pulling heavy inspiration from the iconic Nike Shox R4. Its sleek leather upper retains much of the R4’s original DNA, most notably via the squared-off tongue and the small perforated section near the tip of the toe.However, Nike introduces key modern updates to the 2.0 — the lateral Swoosh branding is now seamlessly embossed directly into the premium leather rather than applied as a separate panel, resulting in a cleaner, more streamlined finish.The biggest update sits underfoot. Instead of recreating the original Ovolo’s heel, Nike has opened up the architecture further, creating more negative space between the raised heel structure and the outsole for a lighter, more exaggerated profile.
